title: Safe and Sustainable by Design (SSbD): a literature landscape and descriptive mapping
content: The European Commission/Joint Research Centre (EC/JRC) Safe and Sustainable by Design (SSbD) framework aims to align chemical and material innovation with safety, sustainability, and policy ambitions. Yet, how SSbD is represented in the scientific literature remains unclear. This review maps SSbD-referencing publications published between 2024 and early 2026. A corpus of 109 publications was classified based on publication type. Of these, 30 publications were identified as evidence-based SSbD-related studies because they reported case-specific results for a chemical, material, process, product, technology or application and were analysed in more detail. The review shows that SSbD literature includes both conceptual contributions and operational building blocks, including early-stage screening, warning flags, sector-specific adaptations, multi-criteria decision support, FAIR data infrastructures, digital tools, and innovation-management approaches. In the evidence-based studies, reported coverage differed across the three SSbD dimensions. Safety was most consistently addressed, followed by environmental sustainability, while socio-economic sustainability remained less frequently represented. Evidence was concentrated in advanced-material contexts, particularly inorganic, hybrid, multicomponent, nano-enabled, polymeric, and carbon-based systems, which is highly relevant given the growing policy focus on advanced materials, digital infrastructures and substitution-oriented innovation support. Safety-related information often addressed selected parts of the hazard-exposure-risk logic, while scoping-related aspects, life-cycle framing, documentation and decision traceability were inconsistently reported. Overall, the review suggests that SSbD is not only cited as a guiding principle but is also increasingly associated with practical questions about how evidence is generated, structured, connected and reported across innovation contexts. Minimum reporting practices, FAIR data, and traceable decision workflows could help distinguish between conceptual reference, partial contribution and practical SSbD innovation capability.
